chapters.n: The book opens with a funeral cry: “How…!” Jerusalem, once crowded and honored among nations, now sits empty like a widow and pays tribute to a foreign master. Chapters 1–4 are acrostic poems, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

f.g: Hebrew ’ekah, the book’s Hebrew title; a typical opening for a funeral dirge (compare Isaiah 1:21).
Forced to pay tribute; reduced to a servant state.

chapters.n: Jerusalem is pictured as a woman weeping alone at night. The “lovers” and “friends” are the foreign allies (like Egypt) Judah trusted instead of the Lord; they gave no help when Babylon came.

f.g: Political allies and foreign gods that Judah courted.

chapters.n: Judah has gone into exile after suffering and hard bondage. Living among foreign nations, she finds no rest; her enemies caught her in a narrow place with no escape.

f.g: In tight places—trapped like prey in a narrow pass.

chapters.n: Even the roads to Jerusalem seem to mourn because no pilgrims travel them for the holy festivals. The temple’s worship has stopped, and priests and young women alike grieve.

f.g: The appointed festivals such as Passover and Tabernacles, when Israel gathered at the temple.

chapters.n: Her enemies are now on top. The poet is honest about why: the Lord allowed this because of Judah’s many sins, just as the covenant had warned.

f.w: her children are gone into captivity

chapters.n: Zion’s glory is gone. Her leaders are like starving deer that can no longer run, fleeing helplessly—perhaps recalling King Zedekiah’s failed escape from the city.

f.g: A poetic name for Jerusalem and its people, personified as a young woman.

f.w: they are gone without strength before the pursuer

chapters.n: In her misery Jerusalem remembers better days. When she fell, no one helped, and her enemies laughed at her ruin, even mocking the sabbaths that marked her as the Lord’s people.

f.g: Some translations read “downfall” or “ceasing”; either way her collapse became a joke to her foes.

chapters.n: The poet does not excuse Jerusalem: she sinned seriously, and so she was removed. Those who once admired her now despise her, seeing her shame exposed.

f.g: A picture of public disgrace and exposure.

chapters.n: Her uncleanness clings to her clothing; she never considered where her choices would lead. Her fall was astonishing. Suddenly Jerusalem herself cries out to the Lord to see her pain.

f.w: she remembereth not her last end
f.g: She did not think about the consequences of her actions.
Astonishingly, in a shocking way.

chapters.n: The enemy has grabbed all her treasures—worst of all, foreigners walked into the temple itself, a holy place the law said they must not enter.

f.w: the heathen entered into her sanctuary

chapters.n: Famine is so severe that people trade their treasures just for food to stay alive. Jerusalem again turns directly to the Lord: “See how worthless I have become.”

f.g: Food of any kind (KJV English).
To keep themselves alive.

chapters.n: One of the most famous lines in Lamentations: Jerusalem calls to passersby, “Is there any sorrow like my sorrow?” Christians have long heard in it an echo of the suffering Savior, whose pain went beyond all others.

f.w: Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by?
the day of his fierce anger

chapters.n: Jerusalem describes judgment as fire in her bones, a hunting net around her feet, and a long sickness that leaves her faint all day long.

f.w: he hath spread a net for my feet

chapters.n: Her sins have become like a heavy yoke the Lord fastens on her neck—sin itself becomes the burden that drags her down into captivity.

f.g: A wooden collar for oxen; a symbol of servitude.

chapters.n: The Lord has crushed her soldiers and young men as grapes are trampled in a winepress. The winepress image of judgment reappears in later scripture concerning the Lord’s coming.

f.w: the virgin, the daughter of Judah
f.g: Poetic title for the people of Judah as a once-protected daughter.

chapters.n: Jerusalem weeps endlessly. The repetition “mine eye, mine eye” shows overwhelming grief. The comforter who should revive her is far away, and her children are ruined.

f.g: One who would bring relief or restore life; the word recurs through this chapter (vv. 2, 9, 17, 21).

chapters.n: The narrator returns: Zion stretches out her hands for help, but no one comes. The Lord has let Jacob’s neighbors become his enemies, and they treat Jerusalem as ritually unclean.

f.g: A gesture of pleading or prayer.
Under the law of Moses, someone ritually unclean and kept apart; here a picture of being shunned.

chapters.n: A turning point of honesty: “The Lord is righteous; I rebelled.” Jerusalem accepts responsibility, the first step of real repentance, and asks the nations to see her suffering.
She called for her allies, but they betrayed her. Even priests and elders died of hunger while searching for food in the besieged city.

f.g: Died.
Searched for food.

chapters.n: Jerusalem cries out in anguish, confessing her rebellion. Outside the city the sword kills; inside, famine and disease bring death—there is no safe place.

f.g: Hebrew idiom: my inner being is in turmoil (the bowels were seen as the seat of emotions).

f.w: abroad the sword bereaveth, at home there is as death

chapters.n: Her enemies rejoice that God has punished her. Yet she trusts that the day of judgment the Lord has announced will come on them too.

f.w: the day that thou hast called
f.g: The day of the Lord’s judgment proclaimed by the prophets.

chapters.n: The poem closes with a plea for justice: let the wickedness of Judah’s enemies come before God as hers has. Her sighs are many and her heart is faint—grief without easy answers.

f.w: Let all their wickedness come before thee

chapters.n: A second acrostic dirge begins with the same cry, “How…!” This time the focus is on the Lord himself as the one who brought the disaster. He has thrown Israel’s glory from heaven to earth and did not spare even the temple, his “footstool.”

f.g: The temple or the ark of the covenant, where God’s presence was said to rest.
Probably Jerusalem and its temple, Israel’s crowning glory.

chapters.n: Without pity the Lord has swallowed up the villages of Jacob and torn down Judah’s fortresses. Kingdom and princes are “polluted”—stripped of their sacred honor.

f.g: The towns and pasture-dwellings throughout the land.
Treated as common or profane; dishonored.

chapters.n: Israel’s “horn” (her strength) is cut off. God has pulled back the protecting right hand that once fought for Israel, and his anger burns like a wildfire.

f.g: A symbol of strength and power, like the horns of a bull.

f.w: he hath drawn back his right hand

chapters.n: The Lord is pictured as an archer aiming at his own people. Those who were most precious are struck down, and his fury pours out like fire on Zion’s “tent.”

f.g: Tent or dwelling; here the city of Zion pictured as a home.

chapters.n: The shocking phrase “The Lord was as an enemy” captures the heart of the chapter. The God who once fought for Israel now seems to fight against her, multiplying her mourning.

f.w: The Lord was as an enemy

chapters.n: God has torn down his own temple as easily as someone pulls down a garden shed. Feasts, sabbaths, king, and priest—Israel’s whole system of worship and government—have been set aside.

f.w: as if it were of a garden
f.g: Like a flimsy booth or hut in a garden or vineyard.
The temple courts where Israel gathered at appointed times.

chapters.n: The Lord has rejected his altar and sanctuary. Enemy soldiers shout in the temple as loudly as worshippers once did at a festival—a bitter reversal.

f.w: they have made a noise in the house of the LORD

chapters.n: Like a builder measuring before demolition, the Lord stretched out a line to tear down Zion’s wall. Ramparts and walls are personified as mourning together.

f.w: he hath stretched out a line
f.g: A measuring line—normally used to build, here used to mark for destruction.

chapters.n: Gates are sunk in rubble, the king is in exile, the law is no longer taught, and prophets receive no vision. Losing revelation is perhaps the deepest loss of all.

f.g: Torah instruction from priests has ceased.

f.w: her prophets also find no vision from the LORD

chapters.n: The city’s elders sit silently on the ground with dust on their heads and sackcloth on their bodies—traditional signs of mourning. Young women bow their heads in grief.

f.g: Rough goat-hair cloth worn as a sign of mourning or repentance.

f.w: cast up dust upon their heads

chapters.n: The poet himself breaks down in tears. In Hebrew thought the liver and bowels were the seat of deep feeling; his whole inner self is poured out because children are fainting in the streets.

f.w: my liver is poured upon the earth
f.g: An idiom for utter emotional collapse.
Nursing infants.

chapters.n: A heartbreaking scene: starving children ask their mothers for food and die in their arms. The poem refuses to look away from the human cost of sin and war.

f.g: Grain (in KJV English “corn” means grain generally, not maize).

chapters.n: The poet searches for a comparison to comfort Jerusalem but finds none; her wound is as vast as the sea. “Who can heal thee?”—a question the rest of scripture answers with the Lord himself.
False prophets had promised peace instead of exposing sin. Had they called the people to repentance, the exile might have been avoided. Their messages led straight to banishment.

f.w: Thy prophets have seen vain and foolish things for thee

f.g: Prophetic oracles or messages.

chapters.n: Passersby clap, hiss, and shake their heads in mockery: is this the city once called “the perfection of beauty, the joy of the whole earth”?

f.w: The joy of the whole earth

chapters.n: Enemies gloat with open mouths and gnashing teeth: “We swallowed her up—this is the day we were waiting for!” (In Hebrew, verses 16 and 17 swap their expected alphabet order, as in chapters 3 and 4.)

f.g: A gesture of hatred and contempt.

chapters.n: The real explanation: the Lord has carried out what he warned long ago through Moses and the prophets. The covenant curses were not random—they were promised consequences.

f.w: he hath fulfilled his word that he had commanded in the days of old

chapters.n: The poet urges the city’s wall itself to weep day and night without rest. Turning to the Lord in tears is the beginning of hope.

f.g: The pupil of the eye; here meaning “do not let your eyes stop weeping.”

chapters.n: “Pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord.” Zion is invited to pray honestly and persistently through the night for her starving children.

f.g: The start of each night watch; ancient nights were divided into watches (three in Israelite reckoning).

f.w: lift up thy hands toward him

chapters.n: Zion speaks directly to God: look at what has happened! The famine was so terrible that mothers ate their own children, and priests and prophets were killed in the temple.

f.w: Shall the women eat their fruit

f.g: About the width of a hand—tiny infants. Some read “children they have cared for.”

chapters.n: Young and old lie dead in the streets. Jerusalem speaks with painful honesty to God, who has not held back in the day of judgment.

f.w: my virgins and my young men are fallen by the sword

chapters.n: God summoned terrors from every side as if calling worshippers to a feast day. No one escaped, and the children Zion raised were consumed—the chapter ends in raw grief.

f.g: Echoes Jeremiah’s repeated phrase magor-missabib, “terror on every side.”
Wrapped as newborns; cared for from infancy.

chapters.n: Chapter 3 shifts to one suffering man speaking for his people. It is a triple acrostic: every three verses begin with the same Hebrew letter. He has felt the “rod” of God’s discipline.

f.g: A shepherd’s or father’s rod, a symbol of discipline; Isaiah calls Assyria “the rod of mine anger.”

chapters.n: Instead of guiding him into light like a shepherd, God seems to have led him into darkness. The man feels his life has been turned upside down.
He feels God’s hand turned against him over and over, all day long—an honest description of how affliction can feel.

f.w: he turneth his hand against me

chapters.n: Grief has aged his body and broken his bones—physical images for deep inner pain.
Like an army building siege works around a city, God has surrounded him with bitterness and hardship.

f.g: A bitter, poisonous herb; a symbol of bitterness.
Toil, hardship.

chapters.n: He feels as if he were buried among those who died long ago, forgotten in darkness.

f.w: as they that be dead of old

chapters.n: Walled in and weighed down with chains, he cannot escape—the experience of a prisoner and of a besieged city.
Even his loud prayers seem to go unheard. Scripture does not hide that faithful people sometimes feel heaven is closed.
His road is blocked with cut stone and his paths are twisted; every route forward seems shut.

f.g: Carefully cut building stone—a solid, deliberate wall.

chapters.n: God feels like a bear or lion waiting in ambush—dangerous and unpredictable from the sufferer’s point of view.

f.w: as a bear lying in wait

chapters.n: He has been dragged off the path and torn apart, left alone and ruined.

f.g: Abandoned, left in ruins.

chapters.n: God is pictured as an archer, and the sufferer as the target.

f.w: set me as a mark for the arrow

chapters.n: The arrows strike deep into his innermost being.

f.g: Kidneys; in Hebrew thought, the seat of the deepest emotions.

chapters.n: His own people laugh at him and make him the subject of their mocking songs—an experience Jeremiah knew personally.

f.w: I was a derision to all my people

chapters.n: He has been forced to swallow bitterness until he feels drunk with it.

f.g: A very bitter plant; a symbol of sorrow and judgment.

chapters.n: As if made to chew gravel and lie in ashes, he feels humiliated and broken.

f.g: Associated with mourning and deep humiliation.

chapters.n: Peace feels far away; he has forgotten what good times were like.

f.g: I forgot what happiness (Hebrew “good”) was.

chapters.n: At his lowest point he concludes that his strength and hope from the Lord are gone. The poem honestly records despair before turning toward hope.

f.w: My strength and my hope is perished from the LORD

chapters.n: He asks God to remember his misery—the bitter “wormwood and gall” of his suffering.
He keeps remembering his pain, and it weighs his soul down.

f.g: Bowed down, sunk low.

chapters.n: The great turning point of the book. He chooses to call something else to mind, and that choice brings hope.

f.w: This I recall to my mind

chapters.n: What he remembers is the Lord’s steadfast love: it is only because of God’s mercies that his people are not completely destroyed, for his compassion never fails.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed—loyal, covenant love that holds on.

chapters.n: God’s mercies are “new every morning”—a fresh supply each day. “Great is thy faithfulness” has become one of the most beloved lines in scripture and hymnody.
Like the priestly tribe of Levi, which received no land because the Lord was their inheritance, he declares that the Lord himself is his portion and hope.
The Lord is good to those who patiently wait for him and seek him.

f.g: To wait in Hebrew (qavah) carries the sense of hopeful expectation.

chapters.n: It is good to hope and wait quietly for the Lord to save—faith that does not demand an immediate answer.
It is good to learn to bear a yoke while young. Trials accepted early can shape strong, humble disciples.
The wise sufferer sits alone in silence, accepting the burden God has allowed rather than raging against it.
Putting one’s face in the dust was a gesture of total humility; he humbles himself in case there may still be hope.

f.w: putteth his mouth in the dust
f.g: Prostrating face-down; complete submission.

chapters.n: He offers his cheek to the one who strikes him and accepts insult. This anticipates the Savior’s teaching and his own patient suffering.

f.w: He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him

chapters.n: The reason for hope: the Lord does not reject forever.

f.w: the Lord will not cast off for ever

chapters.n: Even when he allows grief, he will show compassion because his mercies are abundant.
A tender insight into God’s character: he does not afflict people “from his heart” or take pleasure in their pain. Discipline is not his delight.

f.g: Literally “not from his heart.”

chapters.n: Verses 34–36 form one sentence: God does not approve of crushing prisoners underfoot…

f.g: Captives and the helpless—exactly what exiled Judah had become.

chapters.n: …or of denying someone justice right in front of the Most High…

f.g: A person’s legal rights.

chapters.n: …or of cheating a person in a lawsuit. The Lord sees and disapproves of all such injustice.

f.g: To twist or pervert (a legal case).

chapters.n: Nothing happens unless the Lord allows it. Babylon’s victory was not outside his control.

f.w: Who is he that saith, and it cometh to pass

chapters.n: Both blessing and calamity come within God’s sovereign rule. The Hebrew “evil” here means disaster, not moral wickedness.

f.g: Calamity or misfortune, not sin.

chapters.n: Why should a living person complain about suffering that came because of his own sins? Being alive at all is a mercy.

f.g: Grumble, murmur.

chapters.n: The poem now invites the whole community: let us examine our lives and come back to the Lord. This is the heart of repentance.

f.w: Let us search and try our ways

chapters.n: Lift not only hands but hearts to God—outward prayer joined to inward sincerity.

f.w: lift up our heart with our hands

chapters.n: A frank confession: we sinned and rebelled, and you have not (yet) forgiven.

f.w: We have transgressed and have rebelled

chapters.n: The people describe God’s anger as wrapping around them and chasing them down without pity.

f.g: Pursued, chased.

chapters.n: God seems hidden behind a cloud so prayers cannot get through—the feeling of distance that sin creates.

f.w: that our prayer should not pass through

chapters.n: Israel has become like trash and scrapings among the nations. Paul later uses similar words for how the world treated the apostles.

f.g: Filth scraped off; rubbish.

chapters.n: Enemies open their mouths wide to mock. (This begins a new letter group, matching 2:16.)
Terror, traps, ruin, and destruction have come on them—a string of sound-alike Hebrew words.

f.g: In Hebrew paḥad wa-paḥat, a wordplay; compare Isaiah 24:17.

chapters.n: The speaker’s eyes run with rivers of tears for his ruined people—very like Jeremiah’s own laments.

f.w: Mine eye runneth down with rivers of water

chapters.n: His tears flow without stopping…

f.g: Without a break.

chapters.n: …until the Lord looks down from heaven and sees. Persistent prayer waits for God’s attention.

f.w: look down, and behold from heaven

chapters.n: What he sees of the suffering young women of the city grieves his heart.

f.g: Afflicts, causes pain to.

chapters.n: Enemies hunted him like a bird for no reason—an echo of Jeremiah’s persecution by his own people.
They threw him into a pit to die and sealed it with a stone—strikingly like Jeremiah’s imprisonment in a muddy cistern.

f.g: Hebrew bor, a pit or cistern.

chapters.n: Water rose over his head; he thought, “I’m finished.” Floodwaters are a common biblical picture of overwhelming danger.
From the bottom of the pit he called on the Lord’s name.
Now he speaks with confidence: you heard my voice. He asks God not to close his ear to his gasping cry.

f.g: My gasping or sighing—a prayer too weak for words.

chapters.n: “You came near when I called; you said, ‘Fear not.’” Personal experience of God’s nearness anchors his hope.
The Lord has acted as his defense lawyer and his redeemer. Latter-day Saints see in this the role of Jesus Christ as Advocate and Redeemer.

f.w: thou hast pleaded the causes of my soul

chapters.n: He asks the Lord, who has seen the wrong done to him, to judge his case.
God has seen all the enemies’ revenge and schemes.

f.g: Plots, devices.

chapters.n: The Lord has also heard their insults and plots.

f.g: Taunts, scorn.

chapters.n: He has heard what his enemies say and plan all day long.

f.g: Scheme, plan.

chapters.n: Whether they sit or stand, they sing mocking songs about him.

f.g: Their taunting song (old spelling of “music”).

chapters.n: He asks the Lord to repay his enemies according to their deeds—leaving vengeance to God rather than taking it himself.

f.w: according to the work of their hands

chapters.n: He prays that God will give them hardness of heart and his curse.

f.g: Possibly “hardness” or a “covering” of heart; the Hebrew word is rare.

chapters.n: The chapter ends with a plea for God to pursue and destroy the oppressors. Such prayers leave justice in God’s hands; the Savior later taught his followers to pray even for enemies.

f.w: Persecute and destroy them in anger

chapters.n: The fourth acrostic opens again with “How…!” Gold has lost its shine and sacred stones lie scattered in the streets—pictures of Jerusalem’s lost glory and perhaps of its precious people.

f.g: Literally “holy stones”; possibly temple stones, or a metaphor for the people themselves (see v. 2).

chapters.n: Zion’s children, once valued like pure gold, are now treated like cheap clay jars that are easily broken and thrown away.

f.w: earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter

chapters.n: Even wild animals nurse their young, but famine has made Jerusalem’s mothers unable to care for their children, like the ostrich that was thought to abandon its eggs.

f.g: Probably jackals; the Hebrew tannim is close to the word for jackals.

f.w: like the ostriches in the wilderness

chapters.n: Nursing babies are so thirsty their tongues stick to their mouths; children beg for bread and no one has any to give.

f.g: Breaks bread to share it out.

chapters.n: People who once ate fine food now starve in the streets; those raised in royal purple now cling to garbage heaps. Wealth offered no protection.

f.g: Expensive dyed clothing, a sign of luxury.
Refuse or ash heaps where the destitute sat.

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s punishment seems worse than Sodom’s, which was destroyed in a moment; Jerusalem’s suffering dragged on. Her privileged knowledge made her sin greater.
Her consecrated ones (or princes) were once radiant—whiter than milk, ruddy and healthy, gleaming like precious stones.

f.g: Those set apart by a special vow, or more broadly her nobles. Nazarite vows are described in Numbers 6.
Probably lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone.

chapters.n: Now their faces are blackened and unrecognizable, their skin shriveled on their bones like dry wood. Famine has erased their glory.

f.g: Face, appearance.

chapters.n: Those killed in battle were better off than those who slowly starved to death—a grim measure of the siege’s horror.

f.g: Waste away slowly.

chapters.n: Compassionate mothers boiled their own children for food—the darkest horror of the siege, exactly as Moses had warned would happen if Israel broke the covenant.

f.g: Boiled, cooked.

f.w: The hands of the pitiful women have sodden their own children

chapters.n: The Lord has fully carried out his anger. A fire in Zion has burned down to the foundations—both literally, when Babylon burned the city, and spiritually.

f.w: hath kindled a fire in Zion

chapters.n: No one in the world would have believed Jerusalem could fall. Many in Judah had trusted the temple would make the city untouchable.
The cause of the disaster: the sins of prophets and priests who shed innocent blood—the very leaders who should have guided the people to God.

f.w: For the sins of her prophets
shed the blood of the just

chapters.n: These guilty leaders now stagger through the streets like blind men, stained with blood so that no one will touch their clothing.
People shout at them as they would at lepers: “Unclean! Stay away!” Even among foreign nations they are told they cannot stay.

f.g: Live as a temporary resident.

chapters.n: The Lord himself has scattered them. Since they showed no respect for priests and elders, honor is now withheld from them.

f.g: Scattered them abroad.

chapters.n: “We” now speak: we kept watching for an ally nation—Egypt—to rescue us, but it never could.

f.w: a nation that could not save us

chapters.n: Enemies tracked every step until no one could walk safely; the end had arrived.
The pursuers were faster than eagles, chasing them over the mountains and ambushing them in the wilderness.
King Zedekiah, “the Lord’s anointed,” on whom the people pinned their hopes, was captured as he fled. The phrase “breath of our nostrils” shows how central the king was to national life.

f.g: The Davidic king, here Zedekiah.
Under his protection.

chapters.n: Bitterly, the poet tells Edom to celebrate for now—Edom cheered Jerusalem’s fall—but the cup of God’s judgment will pass to her too.

f.g: Descendants of Esau, southeast of Judah; they helped and gloated over Jerusalem’s fall.

chapters.n: A word of hope: Zion’s punishment is complete, and her exile will not continue forever. Edom’s sins, however, will now be exposed and punished.

f.w: The punishment of thine iniquity is accomplished

f.g: Uncover, expose.

chapters.n: The last chapter is a communal prayer. It has 22 verses like the Hebrew alphabet but is not an acrostic. It begins by asking the Lord to remember and look at his people’s disgrace.

f.g: Shame, disgrace.

chapters.n: The land God gave Israel as an inheritance now belongs to foreigners. Losing the land felt like losing the covenant promise itself.

f.g: The promised land, divided among the tribes as a permanent family inheritance.

chapters.n: Like orphans and widows—the most vulnerable people in ancient society—they have no protector.
They must now buy the water and firewood that once were freely theirs—everyday necessities under foreign control.

f.w: We have drunken our water for money

chapters.n: Pursuers are at their necks; they are worked hard and never allowed rest.

f.w: we labour, and have no rest

chapters.n: “Giving the hand” means making a treaty. Israel had turned to Egypt and Assyria for food and security rather than to God.

f.g: Pledged submission or made an alliance.

chapters.n: Our ancestors sinned and are gone, yet we bear the consequences. Ezekiel 18 will add that each generation also answers for its own choices.

f.w: Our fathers have sinned, and are not

chapters.n: Former slaves—officials of a foreign empire—now rule over them, and no one can rescue them.
Getting food meant risking one’s life because raiders roamed the countryside.

f.g: Bandits and desert raiders.

chapters.n: Starvation fever has scorched their skin as if burned in an oven.

f.g: Hot and blackened, as from fever and famine.

chapters.n: Women in Jerusalem and the towns of Judah were violated by the conquerors—one of the cruel realities of ancient war.

f.g: Raped, violently abused.

chapters.n: Princes were executed and hung up for display, and the elders received no respect.

f.g: Either hanged by the enemy’s hand or hung up by their own hands as a public humiliation.

chapters.n: Young men were forced to grind grain like slaves, and boys staggered under loads of wood.

f.g: Grinding grain at the mill was the work of slaves and captives.

chapters.n: Elders no longer sit at the city gate to judge, and young men no longer play music. Normal community life has stopped.

f.g: The city gate, where elders held court and public business took place.

chapters.n: Joy is gone; dancing has turned to mourning—the reverse of Psalm 30’s praise.

f.w: our dance is turned into mourning

chapters.n: “The crown is fallen”—their honor and kingship are gone. The people take ownership: “Woe unto us, that we have sinned!”

f.w: The crown is fallen from our head

chapters.n: Because of all this their hearts are sick and their eyes are dim with tears.
Mount Zion, the holy hill of the temple, now lies so empty that jackals roam over it.

f.g: Probably jackals, which haunt ruins.

chapters.n: The great statement of faith in the prayer: though the temple lies in ruins, the Lord still reigns forever. God’s throne was never in Jerusalem alone.

f.w: Thou, O LORD, remainest for ever

chapters.n: An honest question: why have you forgotten us for so long? Faith can ask hard questions of God.

The key prayer of the book: “Turn us to you, O Lord, and we shall be turned.” They ask God to begin the change in their hearts. Jewish readers repeat this verse after reading verse 22 so the book ends on hope.

f.w: Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned
renew our days as of old

chapters.n: The book ends with an unresolved question: “Unless you have completely rejected us and are very angry with us.” The answer comes elsewhere in scripture: God promised to gather and restore Israel.

f.w: But thou hast utterly rejected us
f.g: Often translated “unless you have utterly rejected us”—a fearful question rather than a final statement.
